522cad7156b41feed258f5b0f4944c6548c6ec24: Here it is asked: does consciousness not participate in the representation of other bhāvas? Only in the depiction of sāttvika? Further it is said: what is here called "sattva" (consciousness) depends on the state of the mind. The condition for the arising of this state is a concentrated mind, a mind immersed in "samādhi" (calmed). The nature of sāttvikabhāva (tears, horripilation, paralysis, perspiration, and so on) cannot be reproduced while being in any other state of mind. The recreation of the nature of the universe in Nāṭya is possible only under the condition of such a level of consciousness. What example is there for this? It is said here: the states that carry out the purpose of Nāṭya, reproducing now happy, now unhappy events, must be shown from the point of view of flawless consciousness, i.e., in accordance with their true nature. However, how can one who is not unhappy weep while representing grief, and how can one who is unhappy rejoice while showing happiness? Only on the basis of sattva. Therefore this state is called "sāttvikam" (true). It is precisely consciousness that makes it possible to show tears or horripilation regardless of the joyful or sorrowful mood of the performer, therefore these states are called "sattva" (consciousness).

Parātrīśikā is also known as Trikasūtra — the aphorisms of Trika — because it contains teachings that
form the very core of this philosophical system. The themes of this monumental treatise, as
always, are the Supreme Reality and how to realize It, but here Abhinavagupta places emphasis on mantra,
as the reader will yet see. Abhinavagupta's style has always been difficult for most
translators to understand, but this time the bar has been raised to a new height. So for me personally, this will ultimately
be a journey into madness — especially because, added to the difficult translation, there is heavy work:
making the scripture comprehensible (if viewed optimistically) to the ordinary reader through endless explanations.
In short, our voyage, dear reader, may easily turn into the voyage of the mythical "Titanic,"
if we are not careful enough, ha-ha. Well then, to work!

> Hello, again Gabriel Pradīpaka. This is simply the commentary that the very author of Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam — namely Kṣemarāja — wrote to this same scripture. Therefore, my introduction to Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam is for the most part also suitable here. This book is very simple in comparison with the main scripture on Pratyabhijñā — the recognition of the Self — that is, with the famous Īśvarapratyabhijñā of Utpaladeva, which requires a powerful mind to unravel its subtleties. But this does not mean that the commentary on Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam will be without its own difficulties. No, at places it is difficult, as is customary for the scriptures of Trika — but in comparison with the aforementioned treatise (and with others like it) it is completely straightforward. It is like a working manual that quickly leads the seeker to Final Liberation. If you want to know your own divinity as easily as possible — this manual is for you. I am not joking. Having read it, you will no longer be able to miss the recognition of the Self, which is also Final Liberation.
>
> And one more thing: I will only translate this scripture, without giving detailed explanations. If you need a thorough explanation, I advise you to buy the book of the venerable Jaideva Singh. That great translator took upon himself the labor of explaining everything in detail.

> This work was written by the great Master Abhinavagupta and represents a
> concise exposition of Tantrāloka. Tantrāloka is the most important and voluminous work
> of the greatest Master of Trika. Abhinavagupta was also the teacher of the eminent Kṣemarāja
> and lived around 975–1025 CE in Kashmir.
>
> This treatise, named Tantrasāra, is a concise encyclopedia of Tantra.
> Since it is a very advanced text in Trika Shaivism, it is not surprising that a neophyte
> will find it very difficult to understand. To begin to comprehend it, the reader's level
> must be that of a true disciple in Trika.
>
> The goal of life is Liberation. True Liberation constitutes the attainment of His
> Svātantrya, or Absolute Freedom. When Svātantrya of the Great Lord is achieved,
> then you see unity in everything, that is, you cease to see duality as
> before.
>

wrote about forty books, of which the most extensive and the most important is the *Tantrāloka*. In any case,
the present *Parātrīśikāvivaraṇa* is considered the most difficult writing to translate and understand in the entire

intended for very advanced students, as well as for jīvanmukta ⟦0⟧—those liberated
while alive—⟦1⟧, and I am not joking in the least. Hence it is obvious that I will have to add lengthy
explanations, otherwise the reader's boat will be shipwrecked before even leaving the shore.

221-224/ Five vocal defects:
— Kapila: an unnatural voice with a gurgling or phlegmatic quality.
— Unsteady: irregular volume or a thin quality.
— Sandaṣṭa ("bitten"): arising from excessive use of the teeth.
— Kākī ("crow-like"): a harsh quality that fails to achieve proper contact with the vocal registers.
— Tumbakī ("nasal"): a voice associated with nasal resonance.
